lesson.arabic-gender-definiteness.title_en: Masculine and feminine: ة, and the words without it
lesson.arabic-gender-definiteness.family_en: Every noun is masculine or feminine

table.form_en: feminine by meaning, with a ت that isn't ة

steps: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine, things as well as people: قَلَم, pen, is masculine; سَيَّارَة, car, is feminine.
The usual sign of the feminine is ة at the end: طَالِب is a student who's a man, طَالِبَة a student who's a woman.
Some feminine nouns have no ة: some by meaning, like أُمّ, mother; others you simply learn, like شَمْس, sun, and أَرْض, earth.
A word describing a feminine noun takes ة too: الشَّمْسُ كَبِيرَةٌ, the sun is big.
So learn each new noun with its gender, the way you learn its meaning.

examples.en: The mother is a doctor and the father is a teacher.

words.en: (is) a girl (feminine by meaning; its ت is part of the word, not ة)

why.q_en: If شَمْس has no ة, how do I know it's feminine?
why.a_en: From the words that go with it: you say الشَّمْسُ كَبِيرَةٌ, with a feminine describing word, and هَذِهِ, not هَذَا. Dictionaries mark it too. That's why it's worth learning a noun's gender along with the noun.

selftest.why_en: سَيَّارَة ends in ة. قَلَم and بَيْت are masculine.
أَرْض is feminine, even without ة, so its describing word takes ة: كَبِيرَةٌ.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "a teacher" when the teacher is a woman?
selftest.why_en: Add ة: مُعَلِّمَة. مُعَلِّم is a man, and مُعَلِّمَات means several women teachers.

leads_to.en: Describing words take ـَة to match a feminine noun.

lesson.arabic-gender-definiteness.title_en: The article الْـ: sun letters and moon letters

table.form_en: a moon letter: the ل is said
a sun letter: the ل isn't said

steps: الْـ means "the". It's written the same way every time, but it sounds different depending on the letter after it.
Before a moon letter, you hear its ل: الْقَمَر, الْكِتَاب. The ل has a sukūn.
Before a sun letter, the ل isn't said. The next letter is doubled instead, which the shadda shows: الشَّمْس, الدَّرْس.
The sun letters are the ones said with the tip of the tongue: ت, ث, د, ذ, ر, ز, س, ش, ص, ض, ط, ظ, ل, ن. All the others are moon letters.
The spelling doesn't change: the ل stays on the page either way.

examples.en: The sun is in the sky.

words.en: the sun (ش is a sun letter)
the sky (س is a sun letter)
the moon (ق is a moon letter)
tonight (ل is itself a sun letter)

examples.en: The student is in the library.

words.en: the student (ط is a sun letter)
the library (م is a moon letter)

why.q_en: Why isn't الشَّمْس spelled the way it's said?
why.a_en: The spelling keeps "the" the same in every word, so you can always see it. The shadda on the next letter tells you to skip the ل and double that letter instead.

selftest.q_en: In الدَّرْس, is the ل of الْـ said?
choices: No: د is a sun letter
Yes: د is a moon letter
selftest.answer: No: د is a sun letter
selftest.why_en: د is said with the tip of the tongue, so it's a sun letter: the ل is silent and د is doubled.

selftest.q_en: Which word has a moon letter after الْـ?
selftest.why_en: ب is a moon letter, so the ل is said. س and ن are sun letters.

selftest.q_en: What shows that the ل isn't said?
choices: a shadda on the next letter
selftest.answer: a shadda on the next letter
selftest.why_en: The shadda doubles the sun letter in place of the ل. A sukūn on the ل means it is said.

leads_to.en: الْـ is one of several pieces written joined to a word.
How الْـ joins the word before it when you speak.

lesson.arabic-adjective-agreement.title_en: Describing words: after the noun, and matching it
lesson.arabic-adjective-agreement.family_en: An adjective copies its noun: masculine or feminine, الْـ or not

table.form_en: a sentence (الْـ on the noun only)

steps: A describing word comes after its noun: كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ, a new book (literally "book new").
It copies the noun: feminine if the noun is feminine (سَيَّارَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ), and with الْـ if the noun has الْـ (السَّيَّارَةُ الْجَدِيدَةُ).
If only the noun has الْـ, you've made a sentence: السَّيَّارَةُ جَدِيدَةٌ, the car is new.
You can do both at once: السَّيَّارَةُ الْجَدِيدَةُ سَرِيعَةٌ, the new car is fast.
It copies the ending too: in فِي بَيْتٍ قَدِيمٍ, in an old house, both words end in -in.

words.en: the new one (with الْـ: part of the name)
(is) happy (no الْـ: what you say about him)

examples.en: I live in a small flat.

why.q_en: Why does the describing word take الْـ too?
why.a_en: In Arabic a describing word matches its noun in everything: masculine or feminine, الْـ or not, and the ending. الْكِتَابُ الْجَدِيدُ is literally "the book the new". Leaving الْـ off the second word turns it into a sentence: الْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ, the book is new.

selftest.why_en: No الْـ on either word: "a big room". الْغُرْفَةُ كَبِيرَةٌ is "the room is big", and الْغُرْفَةُ الْكَبِيرَةُ "the big room".
The describing word copies the noun: feminine, with ة, and with الْـ.
Only الْوَلَدُ has الْـ, so it's a sentence: the boy (is) happy.

leads_to.en: Where a describing word goes after a chain of nouns.

lesson.arabic-plural-basics.title_en: Plurals: added endings, reshaped words, and "she" for things
lesson.arabic-plural-basics.family_en: Two kinds of plural, and how a plural of things is described

table.form_en: men, or a mixed group: add ـُونَ

steps: Some plurals add an ending: ـُونَ for men or a mixed group (مُعَلِّمُونَ), and ـَات for women and for many things (مُعَلِّمَات, سَيَّارَات).
After a preposition, or as the object, ـُونَ becomes ـِينَ: مَعَ الْمُعَلِّمِينَ, with the teachers.
Many plurals reshape the word inside instead: كِتَاب, كُتُب; بَيْت, بُيُوت. You can't work these out, so learn each plural with its singular.
Things in the plural count as "she": هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ, these are books; الْبُيُوتُ قَدِيمَةٌ, the houses are old.
People in the plural take plural words: هُمْ طُلَّابٌ, they're students.

examples.en: The pens are on the desk.

words.en: new (feminine singular, for a plural of things)

examples.en: The teachers are in the room.

words.en: the teachers (ـُونَ: men, or a mixed group)

why.q_en: Why do things in the plural take "she" words?
why.a_en: That's how Arabic groups them: a plural of things is treated as one feminine whole. So you say هَذِهِ, not هَؤُلَاءِ, and جَدِيدَةٌ, not a plural describing word. هَؤُلَاءِ and plural describing words are for people.

selftest.why_en: بَيْت has a reshaped plural, بُيُوت, which you learn with it.
Pens are things, so the plural takes the feminine singular: جَدِيدَةٌ. جَدِيدُونَ would be for people.

selftest.q_en: Several teachers, all women: which plural?
selftest.why_en: For women, ة becomes ـَات. مُعَلِّمُونَ and مُعَلِّمِينَ are for men, or a mixed group.

leads_to.en: The form for exactly two, and the plurals made with an ending.

lesson.arabic-demonstratives.title_en: This and that: هَذَا, هَذِهِ, ذَلِكَ, تِلْكَ

table.form_en: this (feminine, or things in the plural)
that (feminine, or things in the plural)

steps: هَذَا and هَذِهِ point to something near: هَذَا for a masculine noun, هَذِهِ for a feminine one.
ذَلِكَ and تِلْكَ point to something further away, in the same way.
For people in the plural, use هَؤُلَاءِ (near) and أُولَئِكَ (far). Things in the plural take هَذِهِ and تِلْكَ, as they take "she" words.
هَذَا بَيْتٌ is a sentence: this is a house. With الْـ, هَذَا الْبَيْتُ is just "this house", and needs more to be a sentence: هَذَا الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ.
هَذَا, هَذِهِ, ذَلِكَ and هَؤُلَاءِ are said with a long ā after the first letter, which isn't written as a letter of its own. أُولَئِكَ has one too, after its ل, and its و is silent.

why.q_en: Why is it هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ, not هَؤُلَاءِ, for "these are books"?
why.a_en: هَؤُلَاءِ is only for people. Things in the plural are treated as "she", so they take هَذِهِ: هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ.

selftest.q_en: You point at a car parked far away. Which word do you use?
selftest.why_en: سَيَّارَة is feminine and it's far away, so تِلْكَ. ذَلِكَ is for a masculine noun, and هَذِهِ for something near.
With no الْـ on صُورَةٌ it's a sentence, and صُورَة is feminine, so هَذِهِ. هَذِهِ الصُّورَةُ is just "this picture".

selftest.q_en: Which word points to several people near you?
selftest.why_en: هَؤُلَاءِ is for several people near you, and أُولَئِكَ for several people further away. هَذِهِ is "this" for one feminine noun, or for things in the plural, not for several people.

lesson.arabic-idafa-possession.title_en: Whose is it? كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ and كِتَابِي
lesson.arabic-idafa-possession.family_en: Two ways to show who something belongs to: joining two nouns, or an ending
steps: To say whose something is, put the owner after the thing: كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ is "the book of the student", the student's book.
The first word has no الْـ and no -un ending; the second ends in -i.
For "my", "your", "his" and so on, add an ending to the noun instead: كِتَابِي, my book; كِتَابُكَ, your book.

A word ending in ة says it as t when something follows. If an ending is joined on, it's written ت as well: سَيَّارَتِي, my car. Before a separate word it stays ة on the page: سَيَّارَةُ الْمُعَلِّمِ, the teacher's car.
The pair counts as "the" when the second word has الْـ: بَيْتُ الْمُعَلِّمِ already means "the teacher's house".

examples.en: My neighbour's son is a doctor.
Our house is near the sea.

why.q_en: Why doesn't the first word take الْـ?
why.a_en: The second word already makes the pair definite: كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ is "the book of the student", so "the" is there without الْـ on the first word. The pair works as one unit.

selftest.why_en: The first word has no الْـ and no -un, and the second ends in -i.

selftest.q_en: In سَيَّارَتِي, why is ة written ت?
choices: Because something is added after it
selftest.answer: Because something is added after it
selftest.why_en: When an ending follows, ة is written ت and said t: سَيَّارَة, سَيَّارَتِي.

leads_to.en: Chains of more than two nouns.
